explainer.heading: What happens
explainer.body: A girl writes about her family cruise around Greenland to see the Northern Lights. It was “the most amazing — and terrifying” experience of her life. On a hike on Ella Island a polar bear charged the group; the ranger stopped it with a tranquilliser gun. Back home, the incident started a social-media debate.
explainer.example: Her dream trip: scenery, hiking, wildlife — not Disneyland.

explainer.heading: The journey
explainer.body: They flew London → Reykjavik (Iceland), stayed in a hotel overlooking the harbour and saw green Northern Lights “like a laser light show”. Next they flew to Greenland. The cabin was uncomfortable, but she spent most time on deck. They sailed past steep cliffs and rode a raft between icebergs close enough to touch.
explainer.example: She learned only snow-covered icebergs are white; others look sky-blue.

explainer.heading: The polar bear
explainer.body: On day four, 20 people hiked on Ella Island with a guide and an armed ranger. A thin, bony, furious polar bear appeared. The ranger told everyone to move behind him; adults gathered around the narrator, the youngest. The bear charged; a warning shot made it angrier. Then the ranger used a tranquilliser gun — the bear lay still but was not killed.

explainer.heading: The debate & the writer’s view
explainer.body: Someone posted praise for the ranger. Others were outraged: the group had no right to be in the bear’s territory and polar bears are endangered. The writer’s view: they didn’t expect bears there; bears now come to Ella Island because melting ice stops them finding food in their own habitat. The true cause is climate change and lack of food.
explainer.example: “If the ranger hadn’t stopped the bear, what would have happened?”

explainer.heading: Vocabulary
explainer.body: Words beginning with over- / under-: overlook, overcome, overboard, underestimate, underwater. Similar or different pairs: journey/trip (similar), cruise/voyage. Expressions with “matter”: the fact of the matter, no matter what, a matter of time, as a matter of fact.
explainer.example: As a matter of fact = actually.

explainer.heading: Grammar: have been to / have gone to
explainer.body: Have been to = went and came back (experience). Have gone to = went and is still there / not back yet.
explainer.example: I have been to Greenland (I’m home now). Dad has gone to the market (he is there now).

explainer.heading: Writing: a formal letter
explainer.body: Sender’s address, date, receiver’s designation and address, subject line, salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), body (purpose, details, request), complimentary close (Yours faithfully/sincerely), name. Use polite, formal language; no short forms.
explainer.example: Subject: Request to protect wildlife habitats

Choose correctly: My brother ____ to Delhi; he will return next week.
Choose correctly: I ____ to Mysore three times. It’s lovely!

questions.q: Why did the writer’s parents book the cruise?
questions.model: The writer had always been fascinated by the Northern Lights, so her parents booked a cruise to see them. It also promised scenery, hiking and wildlife, which she loved.
points: She was fascinated by the Northern Lights

questions.q: Explain the difference between “have been to” and “have gone to” with an example each.
questions.model: “Have been to” means someone went and came back, e.g. “I have been to Ooty.” “Have gone to” means someone went and is still there, e.g. “Ravi has gone to Chennai.”
points: Correct meaning + example of “have been to”
Correct meaning + example of “have gone to”

questions.q: Describe the encounter with the polar bear and the debate that followed. Whose view do you agree with and why?
questions.model: On Ella Island a thin, furious polar bear appeared and charged the hiking group. The ranger made everyone stand behind him, fired a warning shot that made the bear angrier, and then used a tranquilliser gun; the bear was not killed. Later, people online praised the ranger, but others said tourists had no right to enter the bear’s territory as polar bears are endangered. The writer says bears come there because melting ice leaves them without food. (Student gives own opinion with a reason, e.g. the ranger was right to protect people safely without killing the bear.)
points: Bear appears and charges; ranger’s actions
Both sides of the debate + writer’s view (melting ice / food)
